money_at_stake.rationale: Nell's card cites Bloomberg (paywalled on fetch, HTTP 403) reporting the depletion; I independently corroborated the underlying claim (deep Tomahawk, Patriot, THAAD and ATACMS/PrSM drawdown from the Iran war, multi-year replenishment) via CNN, Al Jazeera, ABC News, Army Recognition and Defense One, all dated and consistent with Nell's occurrence text, so the occurrence itself stands even though the named outlet did not. On money: the Pentagon's own FY2027 missile procurement request is $70.5bn, a 188 percent jump from FY26's $24.4bn, driven directly by this depletion. Two of the four named systems already carry signed multi-year contracts inside that request: Lockheed Martin's THAAD award (up to $35bn ceiling, 7 years) and Raytheon's Tomahawk award ($22.9bn, 7 years), which is $57.9bn between two of four systems before Patriot and ATACMS/PrSM are added. AEI separately estimates the pure one-for-one replenishment cost of everything expended (interceptors plus roughly two dozen munition types) at over $25bn. These are deliberately not summed into one headline figure, same discipline as IMP-20260830-01: they are a budget request, two ceiling-priced UCAs and an independent think-tank floor estimate, not one addable pool. Held at B10_100 rather than GT_100B because no cited figure for the full four-system replenishment plus base procurement clears $100bn; the $70.5bn FY2027 request is the single most defensible annual figure and it sits mid-band.

public_reach.rationale: Unlike the standing LEAKY example (SIG-20260829-01), every dollar figure found here names a NYSE-listed U.S. prime as the direct recipient: Lockheed Martin (THAAD, up to $35bn), Raytheon / RTX (Tomahawk, $22.9bn) and Northrop Grumman (Patriot and THAAD components, $3bn framework, explicitly brought in to break single-sourcing). No sanctioned, state-owned or private-equity-held recipient appears in any cited award. The one qualification worth carrying to chain time: some interceptor and energetics manufacturing runs through government-owned, contractor-operated plants, and the DefenseScoop source frames rocket motors as a supply bottleneck the Pentagon is deliberately opening to a second listed supplier rather than a captive unlisted one. Scored 85, not higher, because that GOCO layer's exact split between listed operators and other arrangements is a chain-build question, not something this appraisal resolves.

capture_odds.rationale: Structurally concentrated and qualification-gated: Raytheon is the sole Tomahawk producer, Lockheed the sole THAAD producer, and solid rocket motors, the identified bottleneck, sit with a small handful of suppliers the Pentagon is only now trying to widen from one to two. RTX's five framework agreements use 'a collaborative funding approach designed to preserve upfront free cash flow,' meaning government money helps fund the capex, which protects contractor margin rather than the contractor bearing ramp risk alone, the opposite of the Hanwha/Samsung outcome in the Arctic appraisal. Held at 70, not 85+, because DefenseScoop quotes Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at CSIS, on the Northrop framework calling these 'not contracts; they are agreements to agree' pending congressional appropriation, and the LM THAAD award is an undefinitized contract action with $35bn as a ceiling, not a settled price, so a real slice of the pipeline is priced and public but not yet locked into revenue.

timing_fit.rationale: Spend is already committed and moving, not projected: the Lockheed THAAD award and the Raytheon Tomahawk award are both seven-year contracts already signed in 2026 (THAAD announced June 24, 2026; Tomahawk awarded August 17, 2026), not proposals awaiting appropriation, which places the leading edge of the spend inside, in fact at the start of, the 2 to 5 year window. Not scored above 75 because both are seven-year contracts running past 2032, and a May CSIS assessment cited in reporting describes 'a window of vulnerability for several years until inventories return to their previous levels,' so a real share of the total spend and of the outcome this occurrence is really about (restored readiness) lands past the five-year horizon this repo underwrites. Correction on this re-run: an FY2026 obligation figure (over $842 million) and a specific March 2026 to June 2032 delivery-window date once cited here to the Lockheed release do not appear anywhere in that release on two targeted re-fetches; that evidence item is deleted rather than repaired. The seven-year contract term itself, which the release does state, carries the same conclusion without needing the deleted figures.

anchor_date basis: this CAND- record carries no formal {kind, anchor_date, window} occurrence block (method section 0), only occurrence.source_date. anchor_date is set to that source_date (2026-08-29), the most recent dated reporting establishing the occurrence, consistent with check_impact.py's CAND- handling, which requires the id to resolve but does not compare anchor_date for candidate rows the way it does for signals.

PRIME here is a ranking signal, not a verdict: it says this occurrence clears the money, reach, capture and timing bar for a chain build to be worth running, nothing more. Ron's taste rules (TASTE-001, TASTE-002) do not name this occurrence or its family; no filter applied. Chain-build note for whoever runs it: the un-crowded links per Nell's own dimensions sit at solid rocket motors, energetics/explosive fill, large forgings/castings and specialty seekers, not at the primes (RTX, LMT, NOC), which are already exhaustively covered.
